stem: The law of diminishing MRTS says that:
choices: Output falls as more of an input is used
For every unit decrease in one input, increasing amounts of the other input are needed to keep output the same
The isocost line gets flatter as the budget grows
Each worker adds less output than the one before
explain: That is the slides' definition (p. 16). Each worker adding less is diminishing marginal returns, related but a different concept.

stem: Which production function's isoquants show a diminishing MRTS?
explain: Cobb-Douglas MRTS = bK/(aL) falls as L rises. Linear MRTS is constant and Leontief MRTS is undefined.

stem: True or false: A diminishing MRTS is what makes Cobb-Douglas isoquants convex (bowed toward the origin).
explain: True. The slope flattens as you move right, which is the convex shape.

stem: True or false: A linear production function obeys the law of diminishing MRTS.
explain: False. Linear MRTS = b/a is constant at every point.

stem: The S16 slides explain the law of diminishing MRTS by pointing to:
explain: As you add more of one input its marginal product falls, so it takes more and more of it to replace the other input (slide p. 19).

stem: Moving down and to the right along a convex isoquant (more L, less K), the MRTS:
explain: With more labor and less capital, MP_L falls and MP_K rises, so MP_L/MP_K falls.

stem: Points on one isoquant (Q = 100): A (L = 4, K = 3), B (L = 3, K = 4), C (L = 2, K = 6), D (L = 1, K = 9). How many units of capital replace the unit of labor given up going from C to D?
explain: K rises from 6 to 9 when L falls from 2 to 1: 3 units of capital. From A to B it took only 1. That growing amount is the law of diminishing MRTS.

stem: \(Q = K^{0.5}L^{0.5}\) along the isoquant Q = 20 (so K = 400/L). What is the MRTS at L = 10?
Same isoquant (Q = 20, K = 400/L). What is the MRTS at L = 40?
explain: K = 400/40 = 10. MRTS = 10/40 = 0.25. It fell from 4 at L = 10 to 0.25 at L = 40: diminishing MRTS.

stem: A restaurant replaces cooks with kitchen robots one at a time. The first robot replaces 4 cooks, the next replaces 3, then 2. This pattern reflects:
explain: Each additional unit of capital replaces less labor: the substitution rate falls. Constant MRTS would mean every robot replaces the same number.

stem: Why do most firms use some of both capital and labor instead of going all-in on one?
choices: With diminishing MRTS, replacing the last bits of one input takes huge amounts of the other
explain: As one input gets scarce it becomes very hard to replace, so the cheapest mix uses some of both. Isocosts are straight lines. Perfect substitutes would allow all-in.

stem: A firm's isoquant is a straight line. A consultant warns about diminishing MRTS as it automates. Is the warning relevant?
choices: No, a straight-line isoquant means a constant MRTS
No, because the MRTS is undefined
Yes, every isoquant has diminishing MRTS
Yes, because the isoquant slopes down
explain: A straight-line isoquant (linear production) has a constant MRTS. Downward slope alone does not imply diminishing MRTS. Undefined MRTS is Leontief.

stem: True or false: Along a Cobb-Douglas isoquant, the MRTS is higher where the firm uses little labor and lots of capital.
explain: True. MRTS = bK/(aL) is large when K is large and L is small, which is the steep upper left of the isoquant.

stem: Klarna's AI assistant handles routine chats well, but disputes and fraud still need a person. As Klarna replaces more agents with AI, what does diminishing MRTS predict?
choices: Each additional agent removed takes more AI hours to replace
AI hours replace agents at a constant rate
Each agent removed takes fewer AI hours to replace
Output rises as agents are removed
explain: The last agents handle the hard cases the AI is worst at, so replacing them takes more and more AI hours. A constant rate would mean perfect substitutes.
